sources.claim_locator: Sections 9 (Method Definitions), 15 (Status Codes), and 6.4.1 (Content Semantics).
sources.source_claims_supported: Defines HTTP request method semantics and response status codes; explains that request and response content semantics depend on method, status code, and response fields. Supports HTTP request/response behavior, not the broader proposition that every API must have authentication, authorization, gateways, or persistence.
sources.source_limitations: A protocol specification, not implementation guidance for every API architecture. It does not establish that every API requires authentication, authorization, a gateway, or a persistence layer.

sources.claim_locator: Introduction; Paths Object; Path Item Object; Operation Object; Responses Object; Security Scheme Object; version history entry 3.1.1.
sources.source_claims_supported: Defines OpenAPI as a language-agnostic interface description for HTTP APIs; an OpenAPI Description formally describes an API surface and semantics and can support documentation, code generation, and testing. Its Paths and Operation structures describe API operations; security schemes describe declared security. Supports explicit API interface documentation, but does not require that all APIs use OpenAPI or a gateway or persistence.
sources.source_limitations: Describes an API rather than requiring a particular implementation, deployment topology, gateway, or persistence layer. Security scheme declaration does not establish that a particular scheme is adequate.

sources.claim_locator: Risk Description, API2:2023 Broken Authentication; API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization; API10:2023 Unsafe Consumption of APIs.
sources.source_type: Security risk guidance / project web page
sources.source_claims_supported: The 2023 API risk descriptions identify broken authentication and broken function-level authorization as API security risks; API10 explains that developers may trust third-party API data too much and use weaker security standards, enabling attacks through integrated services. Supports security risks and the need to address them, not a universal prescribed API architecture.
sources.source_limitations: Risk taxonomy and explanatory guidance, not a protocol or normative implementation standard. This cited page is the API Top 10 risk description and does not by itself prescribe a complete authentication or authorization design.

sources.claim_locator: Page heading and opening scope; Implementation guidance; Common anti-patterns; closing implementation guidance
sources.source_claims_supported: AWS Well-Architected guidance compares monolith, SOA, and microservices segmentation. It describes potential microservice latency, distributed debugging/tracing and operational costs; calls tightly interdependent service meshes an anti-pattern; says monoliths should be rare and modular/evolvable; and recommends SOA or microservices when the workload and organization can support them. This supports conditional tradeoff analysis, not a universal modular-monolith default.
sources.source_limitations: AWS-specific advisory guidance, not a universal architecture rule or quantified cost model. The page expresses a preference for SOA/microservices when organizational and workload capability permit, while recognizing monoliths as rare cases; a modular-monolith-first recommendation is a separate cross-source synthesis.

sources.source_claims_supported: The official IEEE catalog lists ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207-2026 as an active standard, states that it supersedes 12207-2017, and lists board approval on 2026-02-12 and publication on 2026-04-15. The catalog abstract describes a common software life-cycle process framework and says users may compose a suitable life-cycle model from selected processes/stages.
sources.source_limitations: Catalog status and abstract only; the full normative clauses were not inspected. This does not establish which clauses an organization adopted, whether the standard is contractually or legally binding for a project, or whether any implementation conforms.

sources.claim_locator: Sections 2-3; PO/PS/PW/RV practice headings, especially PW.1, PW.5, PW.7-PW.8 and RV.1-RV.3
sources.source_claims_supported: SSDF is recommended high-level guidance integrable into SDLCs; covers security requirements/risk modeling, code protection, secure coding/review/testing, release integrity and vulnerability response.
sources.source_limitations: Guidance, not universal mandate unless adopted by policy, contract or regulation. Does not define universal stage gates.

sources.claim_locator: Sections 9 (Method Definitions), 15 (Status Codes), and 6.4.1 (Content Semantics).
sources.source_claims_supported: Defines HTTP request method semantics and response status codes; explains that request and response content semantics depend on method, status code, and response fields. Supports HTTP request/response behavior, not the broader proposition that every API must have authentication, authorization, gateways, or persistence.
sources.source_limitations: A protocol specification, not implementation guidance for every API architecture. It does not establish that every API requires authentication, authorization, a gateway, or a persistence layer.

sources.claim_locator: Introduction; Paths Object; Path Item Object; Operation Object; Responses Object; Security Scheme Object; version history entry 3.1.1.
sources.source_claims_supported: Defines OpenAPI as a language-agnostic interface description for HTTP APIs; an OpenAPI Description formally describes an API surface and semantics and can support documentation, code generation, and testing. Its Paths and Operation structures describe API operations; security schemes describe declared security. Supports explicit API interface documentation, but does not require that all APIs use OpenAPI or a gateway or persistence.
sources.source_limitations: Describes an API rather than requiring a particular implementation, deployment topology, gateway, or persistence layer. Security scheme declaration does not establish that a particular scheme is adequate.

sources.claim_locator: Risk Description, API2:2023 Broken Authentication; API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization; API10:2023 Unsafe Consumption of APIs.
sources.source_type: Security risk guidance / project web page
sources.source_claims_supported: The 2023 API risk descriptions identify broken authentication and broken function-level authorization as API security risks; API10 explains that developers may trust third-party API data too much and use weaker security standards, enabling attacks through integrated services. Supports security risks and the need to address them, not a universal prescribed API architecture.
sources.source_limitations: Risk taxonomy and explanatory guidance, not a protocol or normative implementation standard. This cited page is the API Top 10 risk description and does not by itself prescribe a complete authentication or authorization design.
